title: TCP U1·W4 — Entity Choice & Business Tax Planning (2026)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the structure decides the tax

For a business owner, no single decision affects lifetime tax more than entity choice. Whether Meridian Building Group operates as a sole proprietorship, partnership/LLC, S corporation, or C corporation determines how income is taxed, whether the owner gets the QBI deduction, how much flows to payroll taxes, and what happens on sale. This capstone week compares the entities on the 2026 Public Law 119-21 baseline and works the planning levers — especially the reasonable-compensation trade-off that defines S-corporation strategy.

The four entity types

Four structures dominate. A sole proprietorship reports on Schedule C; all profit is the owner's and bears self-employment tax. A partnership/LLC is a pass-through with flexible allocations; active partners owe SE tax, and a partner's basis includes a share of entity debt. An S corporation is also a pass-through but with restrictions (≤100 shareholders, one class of stock, eligible owners) and a defining feature: the owner takes a salary (subject to payroll tax) plus distributions (not subject to SE/payroll tax). A C corporation is a separate taxpayer at a flat 21%, with profits taxed again as dividends to shareholders — the classic double taxation.

Pass-through versus C corporation

The central trade-off is single versus double taxation. Pass-throughs (sole prop, partnership, S corp) are taxed once at the owner level and qualify for the 20% §199A QBI deduction, a large advantage on the 2026 baseline. A C corporation pays 21% at the entity level and again when earnings are distributed as dividends (taxed at 0/15/20% plus the 3.8% NIIT), but it offers a low, stable entity rate for earnings retained and reinvested, fully deductible fringe benefits for owner-employees, and (for qualifying stock) the §1202 QSBS gain exclusion on sale. The C corp wins when earnings are reinvested rather than distributed; the pass-through wins when profits flow to the owner currently.

The reasonable-compensation lever

The signature S-corporation planning move exploits that distributions are not subject to payroll/SE tax while wages are. An owner who takes a modest salary and larger distributions saves payroll tax on the distribution portion — but the salary must be reasonable for the services performed, and the IRS aggressively recharacterizes too-low salaries as wages. The plan is further constrained because the QBI wage limit (Week 2) rewards paying W-2 wages above income thresholds. So reasonable compensation is a balance: low enough to cut payroll tax, high enough to be defensible and to support the QBI deduction — the kind of optimization TCP tests.

Owner-level taxes and basis limits

How owners are taxed on their share differs by entity. Sole proprietors and general/active partners pay self-employment tax (~15.3% up to the wage base, plus Medicare above) on business earnings; S-corporation shareholder-employees pay payroll tax only on wages. Pass-through owners can deduct losses only to the extent of basis and at-risk amounts (and within the passive activity rules) — and a key difference is that a partner's basis includes a share of partnership debt while an S-corporation shareholder's basis does not include entity-level debt (only direct loans to the corporation). This basis distinction frequently decides how much loss an owner can currently deduct.

Methods, plans, and benefits

Entity planning includes several recurring choices. The accounting method — cash (simpler, defers income until received) versus accrual — affects timing; many small businesses use cash, while larger ones or those with inventory may be required to accrue. Retirement plans (SEP-IRA, solo 401(k), defined-benefit plans) let owners deduct large contributions and defer tax. Fringe benefits are most favorable in a C corporation, where owner-employee health and other benefits are fully deductible without the limitations that apply to >2% S-corporation shareholders. Each choice is a lever the planner sets to fit the owner's cash needs and tax position.

The exit and the synthesis

Finally, planning must anticipate the exit. Selling a C corporation as stock can qualify for the §1202 QSBS exclusion (tiered 50/75/100% by holding period on the 2026 baseline), while buyers prefer an asset sale for a stepped-up basis — a tension that shapes deal structure and the double-tax cost of a C-corp asset sale. The synthesis across TCP Unit 1: integrate the individual formula, the QBI deduction, payroll and SE taxes, the wealth-transfer plan, and the entity structure into one optimization that minimizes the owner's total tax over the life of the business — the integrative judgment that defines the discipline.

Formation and conversion

How an entity is formed and changed carries tax consequences. Contributing appreciated property to form a corporation is generally tax-free under §351 (when contributors control ≥80% afterward), and to a partnership under §721 — deferring gain into a carryover basis. Converting entities is asymmetric: electing S status for an existing C corporation is straightforward but carries built-in gains exposure for a recognition period, while liquidating a C corporation or distributing appreciated property can trigger gain. Because entity choice is hard to undo cheaply, the initial structure decision deserves the multi-year analysis this unit teaches.

State and multistate tax

Entity planning is not only federal. State income taxes, franchise taxes, and nexus rules vary widely, and a contractor working across state lines may owe tax in several states based on apportionment of its income. Many states also enacted pass-through-entity (PTE) tax elections that let the entity pay (and deduct) state tax to work around the federal SALT cap — a planning option that interacts directly with Week 2's SALT discussion. The integrated planner weighs the state cost alongside the federal entity choice, because the lowest-federal-tax structure is not always the lowest total tax.

CMA bridge

Choosing and operating MBG's entity is exactly the CFO's tax-strategy seat: setting Jordan Reed's reasonable salary against distributions, preserving the QBI deduction, funding a retirement plan, and structuring an eventual sale for QSBS treatment. The CFO who models entity tax, owner QBI, payroll, and exit together — not as separate problems — captures the integrated savings TCP is built to teach.

Practice and recap

  1. Compare entities: sole prop / partnership-LLC / S corp (pass-through, single tax, QBI) vs C corp (21% + dividend double tax, but retained-earnings rate, fringe benefits, QSBS).
  2. Apply the reasonable-compensation lever (S corp wages vs distributions): low enough to cut payroll tax, high enough to defend and support the QBI wage limit.
  3. Know owner taxes/basis: SE tax on sole props/active partners; partner basis includes entity debt, S-corp shareholder basis does not.
  4. Set accounting method (cash vs accrual), retirement plans, and fringe benefits (best in a C corp); plan the exit (asset vs stock; §1202 QSBS).

Recap: entity choice drives lifetime tax — pass-throughs (sole prop, partnership, S corp) are taxed once and earn the 20% QBI deduction, while a C corporation pays a flat 21% plus dividend tax (double taxation) but offers a low retained-earnings rate, deductible fringe benefits, and the §1202 QSBS exclusion on sale; the defining S-corp lever is reasonable compensation (distributions escape payroll tax, but salary must be defensible and supports the QBI wage limit); owner-level SE tax and the basis rules (partner basis includes entity debt; S-corp basis does not) govern current loss deductions; and the discipline's synthesis is integrating the individual formula, QBI, payroll/SE taxes, wealth transfer, and entity structure into one total-tax optimization.

Pass-through: single tax + 20% QBI deduction. C corp: 21% entity + dividend tax (double), but low retained-earnings rate, deductible fringe benefits, §1202 QSBS on sale. C corp wins when earnings reinvested.
Distributions avoid payroll/SE tax; wages do not. Take salary low enough to save payroll tax but high enough to be reasonable (IRS scrutiny) and to support the QBI wage limit.
Sole proprietors and active/general partners pay SE tax (~15.3% to the wage base + Medicare). S-corp shareholder-employees pay payroll tax only on wages, not distributions.
A PARTNER's basis includes a share of partnership debt. An S-CORP shareholder's basis does NOT include entity-level debt (only direct shareholder loans). Affects deductible losses.
Cash (simpler, defers income to receipt) vs accrual (required for larger firms / inventory). A timing lever in entity planning.
Most favorable in a C corporation (owner-employee benefits fully deductible). >2% S-corporation shareholders face limits on several fringe benefits.
C-corp STOCK sale may qualify for §1202 QSBS exclusion (tiered 50/75/100% by holding period, 2026); buyers prefer ASSET sales for step-up, raising the double-tax cost of a C-corp asset sale.

questions.q: A defining tax feature of a C corporation is:
choices: Double taxation (21% entity tax, then dividend tax)
questions.explain: C-corp earnings are taxed at 21% and again as dividends — double taxation; pass-throughs get QBI instead.

questions.q: The 20% §199A QBI deduction is available to owners of:
choices: Pass-through entities (sole prop, partnership, S corp)
questions.explain: QBI applies to pass-through business income, not C-corporation income.

questions.q: The S-corporation reasonable-compensation strategy works because:
choices: Distributions are not subject to payroll/SE tax, but wages are
questions.explain: Shifting income from wages to distributions cuts payroll tax — but the salary must be reasonable and supports the QBI wage limit.

questions.q: A partner's basis, unlike an S-corporation shareholder's, includes:
choices: A share of the entity's debt
questions.explain: Partnership basis includes a share of entity debt; S-corp shareholder basis does not (only direct shareholder loans).

questions.q: Owner-employee fringe benefits are MOST favorably deductible in a:
questions.explain: C corporations fully deduct owner-employee fringe benefits; >2% S-corp shareholders face limits.

questions.q: Active general partners and sole proprietors owe self-employment tax on:
questions.explain: Sole proprietors and active partners pay SE tax on business earnings; S-corp distributions avoid it.

questions.q: A C corporation generally becomes more attractive than a pass-through when earnings are:
choices: Retained and reinvested rather than distributed
questions.explain: The flat 21% rate favors retained, reinvested earnings; distributing triggers the second (dividend) tax.
